newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Tennis-Fans back Pierce, Asians lose out. [CORRECTED 11:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Tennis-Fans back Pierce, Asians lose out. [CORRECTED 11:30 GMT]

text.p: Former champion Mary Pierce roused the crowd with a touch of the old magic on Friday (corrects from Thursday) as two Australian Open hopefuls from Asia fell by the wayside.
On a day which belonged to the tournament's dark horses, Spain's Carlos Moya blasted his way into the last 16 and Andrei Medvedev of Ukraine joined him with a 6-1 6-1 6-1 win.
Top seed Steffi Graf survived a brief scare for the second time in the tournament, but came from 1-4 down in the first set to beat Argentine Ines Gorrochategui 7-5 6-3.

Graf, whose father is on trial in Germany on tax evasion charges, confirmed she was helping tennis authorities investigate allegations that she received appearance money in the early 1990s against tour rules.

Born in Canada, based in the United States and playing for France, Pierce had Australia on her side when she met Marketa Kochta of Germany on an outside show court. The Open has drawn record crowds in its first week though home players have been a disappointment.
The match itself took a mere 48 minutes, Pierce calmly disposing of the German 6-0 6-2 to underline her comeback from long-running morale and injury problems.
Her departure from court was the complicated part. Among the host of autograph hunters was a young man with a Mohican haircut who asked Pierce to sign his head.

Pierce's next opponent will be fifth seed Anke Huber of Germany, who lost in last year's final to Monica Seles and was beaten by Pierce in the fourth round in 1995. Huber beat Natasha Zvereva of Belarus 7-5 6-0.
Spain's Moya, who beat defending champion Boris Becker in a first-round upset, made short work of Germany's Bernd Karbacher, winning 6-2 6-2 6-2 before a big crowd of largely female fans.
His brow wrapped in a bandana, the new tournament heart-throb hardly seemed to raise a sweat as he disposed of Karbacher in just over an hour.

But the most impressive performance in the men's draw came from unseeded Medvedev, who took only 70 minutes to beat Dutchman Dennis Van Scheppingen after ousting 15th seed Michael Stich of Germany in five sets on Wednesday.
Ranked as high as number four in the world in 1994, Medvedev has seen his ranking slump to 36 in the world due to persistent injury problems.
Those are now behind him and the 1.92-metre (six foot four inch) tall Ukrainian now faces either world number two Michael Chang or Britain's rising star Tim Henman in the fourth round.
"They should know that they will have to struggle, that they will have to bleed," Medvedev warned his future opponents.
While the big names prospered, two Asian grand slam hopes sank. Seventh seed Lindsay Davenport beat Thailand's Tamarine Tanasugarn 6-1 6-0 in just 44 minutes.
The 19-year-old from Bangkok had already notched up her country's best grand slam run by the time she reached up to shake hands with the towering 1996 Olympic gold medallist.
And Japan's Rika Hiraki -- her country's best hope to succeed Kimiko Date as the region's best player -- spent exactly an hour on court before losing 6-2 6-2 to American Kimberly Po.
British grand slam hopes remained alive ahead of Friday's night-time feature match between Henman and Chang.

Henman, who has emerged one of Britain's most promising players since the great Fred Perry won three consecutive Wimbledons in the 1930s, was quoted by Australian bookmakers as a 9-4 chance to beat the former French Open champion Chang.
